title: The Crypto Shelf and the Open Wire: a Reader with No Department
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Washington, D.C., the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the last summer of the war a son is born in Washington to Bailey Wallys Diffie, professor of Iberian history and culture at the City College of New York, and to Justine Louise Whitfield, writer and scholar. No source reached names the hospital, and the coordinate marks the city only. The family will settle in Queens within a few years, but the birth itself belongs to this city. Thirty miles up the road is Fort Meade, where a headquarters not yet built will one day turn this same infant away as a grown man asking questions.
suggested_refs: The canonical Washington, D.C. pin shared with the Levi-Strauss journey

stops.name: Jamaica, Queens, the household
stops.date_confidence: inferred: no source reached dates the family's move to Queens; the year is a default within the attested childhood there
stops.campa: The family lives in Jamaica, Queens, and the father commutes to Harlem to lecture on Iberian and Latin American history. The childhood address is nowhere recorded and the coordinate marks the neighborhood, not a house. What is recorded is the furniture of the household: a historian of the Spanish and Portuguese empires on one side, a scholar and writer on the other, and between them a child who asks questions. The answer that comes back is never a sentence. It is an armful of books fetched off a shelf somewhere else.
suggested_refs: Bailey W. Diffie, Prelude to Empire and Foundations of the Portuguese Empire, the father's published work

stops.name: City College of New York, the crypto shelf
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the episode is dated only by his age, about ten; the year is computed from the birth date
stops.campa: He is about ten years old when he asks his father about secret writing. Bailey Diffie comes home from the Convent Avenue campus with the cryptology shelf of the City College library, the whole of it, and the son reads it through. The lineage is already assembled in those books: Roger Bacon folding the formula for gunpowder into the Opus Tertium, Francis Bacon at seventeen devising a biliteral alphabet so that any text may carry a second text, Charles Barbier's night writing for the field, which Louis Braille takes apart and rebuilds under the fingers. Whitfield Diffie is never enrolled here. The shelf enrolls him.
suggested_refs: The cryptology holdings of the City College of New York library, c. 1954

stops.name: Jamaica High School, the local diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1961; the month is a default for graduation
stops.campa: He finishes at Jamaica High School on Gothic Drive with a local diploma rather than the Regents track. He reads slowly and writes with difficulty, a pattern he later describes in terms consistent with undiagnosed dyslexia; the description is his own and retrospective, and no medical record stands behind it here. Nothing in the transcript forecasts the paper. The boy who does not sit the state examination sequence is admitted to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the autumn.
suggested_refs: Jamaica High School, 167-01 Gothic Drive, Queens, closed 2014

segments.name: Mathematics, and Work for the Contractors

stops.name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the bachelor's degree
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the 1965 bachelor of science is attested, the matriculation date is not; September 1961 is a default
stops.campa: He reads mathematics at MIT and takes the bachelor of science in 1965. He thinks of himself as a pure mathematician, drawn to partial differential equations and topology, and holds computing in open contempt. No course in cryptography is offered to him here, nor anywhere else in his education; he keeps reading the subject privately, a hobby with no department attached to it. Robert Oppenheimer walked this same city as a Harvard undergraduate four decades earlier. Diffie leaves Cambridge in 1965 for a defense contractor outside the city, and goes on reading the subject on his own time.
stops.quote: as very low class... I thought of myself as a pure mathematician and was very interested in partial differential equations and topology and things like that
stops.quote_source: Whitfield Diffie, quoted in Steven Levy, Crypto (2001), as reproduced on the Wikipedia article 'Whitfield Diffie'
suggested_refs: MIT Department of Mathematics course catalogues, 1961-1965

stops.name: MITRE Corporation, Bedford, four years on MATHLAB
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is a default
stops.campa: Out of MIT he goes to the MITRE Corporation at Bedford, a not-for-profit contractor of the kind the Cold War invents to hold work the government wants done outside itself. He is a research assistant on MATHLAB, an early system for symbolic computation, and the work sits near enough to computer security to keep the old hobby breathing. He stays four years. Nothing in the sources records what he made of the defense-contractor setting at the time. What is recorded is that in 1969 he leaves it for California.
suggested_refs: The MATHLAB symbolic computation system, MITRE Corporation, 1960s

stops.name: Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, the hill above Felt Lake
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In November he joins the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory as a research programmer. The laboratory occupies the D. C. Power Building on Arastradero Road, on a hill above Felt Lake some five miles from the main campus, and the building will later be demolished. John McCarthy sets him to LISP 1.6 and to the mathematical proof of correctness of programs. Proving a program correct is one short step from proving a cipher secure, and Diffie takes that step privately, on his own hours, for three and a half years.
suggested_refs: The D. C. Power Building, 1600 Arastradero Road, home of SAIL until 1980

stops.name: Stanford foothills, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In May he quits. No institution funds what he intends to do next, because no institution is doing it: in 1973 the study of cryptography outside the classified world has no journal, no conference, no faculty, and exactly one customer. He loads a car. Mary Fischer, his girlfriend and later his wife, travels with him and helps him work. For the next two years his method is the one he will describe later without any embarrassment at all, and the record of those two years is mostly his own account of them.
stops.quote: I started out driving around the US, looking for anybody who was willing to talk about this subject, digging up rare manuscripts in libraries, and sitting around thinking about it.
stops.quote_source: Whitfield Diffie, ACM A.M. Turing Award oral transcript, amturing.acm.org
suggested_refs: The ACM Turing Award interview transcript, on the years of independent research

stops.name: National Archives, Washington, the declassified shelves
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the road years are dated 1973-1974 in outline, this stop is dated by no source reached; the month is a default
stops.campa: The road brings him back to the city he was born in, to the declassified cryptologic records held on Constitution Avenue. The visit belongs to the legend as Steven Levy tells it in Crypto rather than to any document consulted for this journey, and it is set down here as reconstruction. What the legend claims is modest and entirely plausible: that the education no university would sell him was assembled instead out of paper the government had released and then stopped thinking about.
suggested_refs: Steven Levy, Crypto: How the Code Rebels Beat the Government (Viking, 2001)
sources: Steven Levy, Crypto (2001), recalled narrative; not re-verified page by page

stops.name: George C. Marshall Research Library, Lexington, Virginia
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: undated in any source reached; placed within the 1973-1974 road years
stops.campa: At the Virginia Military Institute in Lexington the Marshall Research Library holds papers connected to William Friedman, the man who built American cryptanalysis and then watched the whole subject vanish into an agency that would not let him discuss his own work. Diffie reads there. The stop is carried by Levy's narrative and was not re-verified against the library's finding aids in this research, so it stands as reconstruction. Friedman's archive is one of the few open doors in a science whose practitioners are all indoors.
suggested_refs: The William F. Friedman Collection, George C. Marshall Research Library
sources: Steven Levy, Crypto (2001), recalled narrative; not independently re-verified

stops.name: Fort George G. Meade, the fence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: widely repeated in popular accounts, undated in any source reached
stops.campa: He seeks contact with the National Security Agency at its own headquarters and is turned away. The agency has grown, in the years since the war, from wartime signals intercept work into the best funded and least examined arm of the American secrecy state, its budget and its charter both classified from the start. The rebuff appears in the popular histories and in no document reached here. Its consequence is not in doubt: whatever he builds, he builds outside.
suggested_refs: Steven Levy, Crypto (2001), on the approach to the NSA

stops.name: Great Neck, Long Island, at David Kahn's house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: undated in any source reached; placed within the road years
stops.campa: In Great Neck he calls on David Kahn, whose Codebreakers of 1967 is the only general history the subject has and was written over the agency's objections. Kahn has already done in public the archival work Diffie is now repeating for himself. The address is unverified and the coordinate marks the town; the visit itself is reconstruction from Levy. Two men who are not cryptographers by employment sit in a house on Long Island and discuss a science whose only employer will speak to neither of them.
suggested_refs: David Kahn, The Codebreakers (Macmillan, 1967)
sources: Steven Levy, Crypto (2001), recalled narrative; address and date unverified

stops.name: Yorktown Heights: the Watson Research Center, and a name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season, summer 1974; the month is a default within it
stops.campa: In the summer he reaches the Thomas J. Watson Research Center on Kitchawan Road, where IBM keeps the only well-funded cryptographers in the country who will receive a visitor off the road. He meets Alan Konheim, who directs the group behind Lucifer, the cipher on its way to becoming the Data Encryption Standard. Konheim is bound by what he cannot discuss and gives him instead the one thing that is not classified: a name. There is a professor at Stanford working the same problem. Go and see Martin Hellman.
suggested_refs: The IBM Lucifer cipher and the drafting of the Data Encryption Standard, 1973-1977

stops.name: Stanford, the half hour that runs into the evening
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1974; the month is a default
stops.campa: Back in California he telephones Martin Hellman and is granted half an hour. The half hour extends over many hours. Hellman is an electrical engineer who has been warned by everyone sensible that cryptography is a dead subject with one customer and no future; Diffie is an unemployed reader who has just been everywhere the subject is written down. They are working the same problem from opposite ends, key distribution as mathematics and key distribution as history. Hellman takes him on. The arrangement is a laboratory of two, and nobody's permission is asked.
suggested_refs: Martin Hellman's later accounts of the first Diffie meeting at Stanford

stops.name: Stanford, the doctorate not taken
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: He enrolls in June as a doctoral student in electrical engineering under Hellman's sponsorship and never takes the degree. The obstacle, in the end, is a required physical examination he does not sit. He stays on as research assistant and part-time programmer through 1978. Ralph Merkle joins the collaboration, having reached the same puzzle independently, and the three of them constitute very nearly the whole of public cryptography in the United States.
stops.quote: I didn't feel like doing it, I didn't get around to it
stops.quote_source: Whitfield Diffie on the unsat physical examination, quoted in Steven Levy, Crypto (2001), as reproduced on Wikipedia
suggested_refs: Ralph Merkle's 1974 Berkeley project on secure communication over insecure channels

stops.name: New York Coliseum, the National Computer Conference
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the venue and the presentation could not be reconfirmed in this research; the November paper is separately attested
stops.campa: At the National Computer Conference on Columbus Circle the two of them put the idea in front of the computing trade some months before the journal prints it: that two strangers on an open wire can agree on a secret without having met, and that the key which locks need not be the key which opens. The conference venue and the presentation are entered here as reconstruction, not attestation. What the room made of it that June is not recorded anywhere reached.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the 1976 National Computer Conference
sources: General histories of the Diffie-Hellman paper; venue not reconfirmed

stops.name: Stanford, New Directions in Cryptography
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication
stops.campa: The paper appears in the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory for November, two authors, eleven pages. It defines the public key cryptosystem, in which the enciphering key may be published while the deciphering key still cannot be computed from it, and it sets out the key exchange that now carries both names. The arithmetic underneath is modular exponentiation in a finite field, the theory of congruences that Carl Friedrich Gauss laid down in the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae of 1801. Gauss's book waits one hundred and seventy-five years for this use.
stops.quote: WE STAND TODAY on the brink of a revolution in cryptography.
stops.quote_source: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory IT-22:6, November 1976, p. 644
suggested_refs: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, vol. IT-22, no. 6, November 1976, pp. 644-654
sources: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography' (1976), read directly

stops.name: Stanford, the sentence that is not mathematics
stops.date_confidence: the closing line belongs to the November 1976 paper; the day here separates this stop from the preceding one and carries no evidential weight
stops.campa: The historical section of the paper closes on a sentence of a different kind. The claim sometimes attached to it, that the agency's monopoly breaks from the moment of publication, does not survive the following fifteen years and is marked overstated here: export control under the arms regulations, the 1977 letter warning symposium speakers that reading their own papers aloud may be an offense, Admiral Inman's push for prepublication review in 1979, the fight over the length of the DES key, and the Clipper Chip of 1993. The paper opens the field. The field is then contested for a generation.
stops.quote: We hope this will inspire others to work in this fascinating area in which participation has been discouraged in the recent past by a nearly total government monopoly.
stops.quote_source: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory IT-22:6, November 1976, p. 654
suggested_refs: The 1977 Meyer letter to ISIT participants; the 1993 Clipper Chip proposal

segments.name: Secure Systems, One Company at a Time

stops.name: Northern Telecom, Mountain View, manager of secure systems research
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He leaves the university without a doctorate and becomes manager of secure systems research at Northern Telecom in Mountain View, where the task is to put key management inside telephone equipment that customers will actually buy. He stays thirteen years. In 1981 the IEEE gives the 1976 paper its Donald G. Fink Prize. The exact office is not recorded and the coordinate marks the town. The pattern of the working life is set here: the research gets done inside companies, because the universities did not want it and the agency would not share it.
suggested_refs: Bell-Northern Research secure systems programme, 1978-1991

stops.name: University of California, Santa Barbara, the CRYPTO conference
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: entered as a recurring pattern across the 1980s and later, not as a dated single visit
stops.campa: Every August the field he opened convenes at Santa Barbara for the conference called CRYPTO, in student dormitories, with a program committee and published proceedings and several hundred people belonging to a profession that did not exist in 1975. Diffie is a recurring presence here and at its European counterpart. The years of his attendance are not itemized in anything reached, so the stop stands as a pattern rather than a date. The subject has acquired the thing it lacked when he quit his job to go looking for it: other people.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of CRYPTO, Springer Lecture Notes in Computer Science, from 1981
sources: General knowledge of CRYPTO conference history; attendance years not itemized

stops.name: Sun Microsystems Laboratories, Menlo Park
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He joins Sun Microsystems Laboratories at Menlo Park as a distinguished engineer and rises over eighteen years to chief security officer, vice president, and Sun Fellow. The campus straddles Menlo Park and Palo Alto across that period and the coordinate is approximate. Sun is where the 1976 arithmetic turns into plumbing: the protocols carrying the Diffie-Hellman exchange into mail, remote login, and the web are written and shipped in these years by engineers who were small children when the paper appeared.
suggested_refs: Sun Microsystems Laboratories technical reports, 1991-2009

stops.name: ETH Zurich, an honorary doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich awards him a doctorate honoris causa. He holds no earned doctorate of any kind; the unsat physical examination of 1975 saw to that. Zurich is the first institution to settle the question of his standing by issuing a document. The work is sixteen years old by then, in daily industrial use across two continents and taught to undergraduates, and no university has yet conferred anything at all on the man who did it.
suggested_refs: ETH Zurich register of honorary doctorates, 1992

stops.name: The Franklin Institute, Philadelphia, the Louis E. Levy Medal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Franklin Institute awards him the Louis E. Levy Medal. The institute was founded in 1824 and named for the printer who put a kite into a thunderstorm, and it has been giving medals for engineering since before engineering was a profession. The year before, he takes the Paris Kanellakis Award; the year after, the Golden Jubilee Award of the IEEE Information Theory Society, whose Transactions printed the paper. The honors now arrive annually, and not one of them yet comes from a government.
suggested_refs: The Franklin Institute awards database, Louis E. Levy Medal, 1997

stops.name: Menlo Park, Privacy on the Line
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: With Susan Landau he publishes Privacy on the Line, a study of the politics of wiretapping and encryption, written while his own government is arguing in court that a cipher strong enough to be useful is a munition. An updated edition follows in 2007. The book states the second half of his career plainly: the mathematics was finished in eleven pages in 1976, and the argument over who is permitted to use it is not finished, and will outlast the people now having it.
suggested_refs: Whitfield Diffie and Susan Landau, Privacy on the Line (MIT Press, 1998; updated ed. 2007)

stops.name: Bologna, the Marconi Prize
stops.date_confidence: the award year is attested; the ceremony city is not established, and the coordinate is a placeholder rather than a claim
stops.campa: The Marconi Society awards him its annual prize. The city of the ceremony for this year could not be established in this research; the coordinate is set at Bologna, the foundation's traditional seat, as a placeholder and is flagged as a gap. Guglielmo Marconi's own invention created the problem the prize now rewards a solution to. Once a message travels through open air, everyone within range receives it, and the only privacy left to it is arithmetic.
suggested_refs: Marconi Society prize records, 2000
sources: Wikipedia, 'Whitfield Diffie'; ceremony location a stated gap

stops.name: Royal Holloway, Egham, the visiting professorship
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He holds a visiting professorship in the Information Security Group at Royal Holloway, University of London, at Egham in Surrey. Two of the accounts gathered for this journey assert an honorary doctorate here as well; neither Royal Holloway's own pages nor any other source reached corroborates it, so the honorary degree is dropped rather than repeated and the disagreement is recorded. The visiting professorship stands. Royal Holloway's own honorary-graduate records list no Diffie at all.
suggested_refs: Royal Holloway Information Security Group, visiting staff listings, 2008
sources: contradicted by two gathered accounts claiming an honorary doctorate

stops.name: Menlo Park, leaving Sun
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: He leaves Sun in November. Oracle's acquisition of the company was announced in April and does not close until the twenty-seventh of January following, so the usual formula, that he departed after the acquisition, reverses the order: he leaves while it is pending. Eighteen years end. He is sixty-five, holds no degree past the 1965 bachelor's, and is about to be handed by a sequence of academies everything an academic career would have supplied to him in advance.
suggested_refs: Oracle's acquisition of Sun Microsystems, announced April 2009, closed 27 January 2010

stops.name: Encina Hall, Stanford, the Center for International Security and Cooperation
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is given as 2009-2010; the month here is a default
stops.campa: He returns to Stanford as a visiting scholar at the Center for International Security and Cooperation in Encina Hall, an institute for the study of arms control and war, which is the correct department for the thing he actually works on. Thirty-six years earlier he walked out of a laboratory five miles up the hill because it would not let him study cryptography. The campus takes him back on the third attempt: research programmer, then failed doctoral candidate, now visiting scholar.
suggested_refs: CISAC visiting scholar rosters, Freeman Spogli Institute, Stanford

stops.name: ICANN headquarters, Marina del Rey
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In May he becomes Vice President for Information Security and Cryptography at ICANN, the body that allocates the names and numbers the internet runs on, then housed at Marina del Rey. The organization relocates to Playa Vista later, and the coordinate follows the tenure rather than the present address. The man who published key exchange takes a post defending the one namespace in which every key exchange has to find the party it is exchanging with.
suggested_refs: ICANN headquarters at Marina del Rey, occupied until the Playa Vista move

stops.name: Alexandria, Virginia: the National Inventors Hall of Fame
stops.date_confidence: the induction year is attested; month and day defaulted, and the ceremony venue for this year is unconfirmed
stops.campa: He is inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame together with Hellman and Merkle, for United States patent 4,200,770, public key cryptography. The hall has occupied the Patent and Trademark Office campus at Alexandria since 2008 and the coordinate marks it, though the annual induction ceremony is a separate event whose venue for this year is not confirmed by anything reached. The patent long ago expired. What it described had by then become the ordinary way strangers speak.
suggested_refs: US Patent 4,200,770, Cryptographic Apparatus and Method, Hellman, Diffie and Merkle
sources: invent.org, National Inventors Hall of Fame, 2011 inductees

stops.name: Computer History Museum, Mountain View, a Fellow
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month is a default for the fellow awards ceremony
stops.campa: The Computer History Museum names him a Fellow. The museum stands on Shoreline Boulevard, a few minutes from the Northern Telecom office where he managed secure systems research for thirteen years, and about seven miles from the hill where he resigned from the artificial intelligence laboratory. Silicon Valley has built itself an institutional memory and is now installing him inside it while he is alive, alongside machines that sit behind glass and are switched off.
suggested_refs: Computer History Museum Fellow Awards, 2011

stops.name: Marina del Rey, the ICANN term ends
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: The ICANN appointment ends in October after two and a half years. It is the only post he holds in his life at an institution that governs anything, and the thing it governs is an address book: the register of names and numbers without which no two machines can find each other in order to begin the exchange he invented. He is sixty-eight. No account reached explains the departure, and the silence is left standing as a silence rather than filled in with a plausible reason.
suggested_refs: ICANN staff announcements, October 2012

stops.name: Stanford, consulting scholar
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is given as 2012 to the present; the month is a default
stops.campa: He takes a continuing appointment as consulting scholar at Stanford and holds it still. The working life is legible now from end to end: four years at a defense contractor, four at an artificial intelligence laboratory, two with no employer at all and a car, three at a university that never gave him a degree, thirteen at a telephone company, eighteen at a computer company, thirty months at ICANN, and a desk at the institution where the paper was written.
suggested_refs: Stanford Center for International Security and Cooperation, affiliated scholars

stops.name: San Francisco, the Turing Award banquet
stops.date_confidence: the 2015 prize year and the joint award are attested; the June 2016 San Francisco ceremony is reconstruction and was not reconfirmed
stops.campa: The Association for Computing Machinery gives the A. M. Turing Award for 2015 jointly to Diffie and Hellman, for fundamental contributions to modern cryptography. The banquet follows the June after, at a San Francisco venue this research could not reconfirm; the ceremony is entered as reconstruction and the award itself as attested. Forty years separate the paper from the prize. Retrospectives call the recognition belated, and in the interval the invention had become the mechanism by which a few billion people reach a bank.
suggested_refs: ACM A.M. Turing Award citation, 2015, Diffie and Hellman

stops.name: The Royal Society, Carlton House Terrace, Foreign Member
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of election, 2017; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Royal Society elects him a Foreign Member. Two of the accounts gathered for this journey date the election to 2015 and one adds a later promotion to Fellow; both are wrong, and the errors are recorded here rather than quietly repaired. The election falls in 2017, alongside Max Cooper, Robert Grubbs, Hideo Hosono and Marcia McNutt, and Foreign Member is a separate category from Fellow rather than a rung beneath it. The coordinate sits about two hundred metres from Carlton House Terrace.
suggested_refs: Royal Society list of Foreign Members elected in 2017
sources: contradicted by two gathered accounts giving 2015

stops.name: National Academy of Engineering, Constitution Avenue, Washington
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is a default
stops.campa: He is elected to the National Academy of Engineering, on Constitution Avenue, for the invention of public key cryptography. The building stands about two miles from the block where he was born and thirty from Fort Meade. Buckminster Fuller took the Presidential Medal of Freedom in this city in 1983. Washington issues Diffie a membership at seventy-two for work it spent two decades trying to keep unpublished. The city that produced him and the city that obstructed him are the same city.
suggested_refs: National Academy of Engineering member records, class of 2017
sources: National Academy of Engineering member record

stops.name: Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, a visiting professorship
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He takes a visiting professorship at Zhejiang University in Hangzhou. The key exchange he published in 1976 is by now the property of no country, which is what publication means and which the agency at Fort Meade understood in advance of everybody else. An armful of library books carried home in Queens, a car with no funding behind it, and now a lecture hall on the Yuquan campus. Not one point on that line lies inside a classified facility, and the subject that had no department to teach it in 1961 now has a lecture hall on the far side of the world.
suggested_refs: Zhejiang University visiting faculty announcements, 2018

stops.name: Stanford, named a Fellow of the IEEE
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers names him a Fellow. He is eighty. The honors have now run without a gap since 1981, and the man is still alive and still answering his mail, still curious about how a thing is put together. Most completed lives close with a grave to stand at, a relic, a quarrel between two cities over where the bones lie. His does not, not yet: no tomb and no settled fate, only a record that stops here because there is nothing further yet to set down.
suggested_refs: IEEE Fellow class of 2025 citation

stops.name: Stanford, the absent monument
stops.date_confidence: status as of the compilation of this journey, August 2026
stops.campa: As of 2026 there is no statue, no plaque, no building carrying his name. The commemoration is entirely institutional: a Turing Award, a foreign membership, two academies, a hall of fame, a museum fellowship. The monument, if the word is wanted, is a handshake performed some trillions of times a day by machines that do not know whose arithmetic they are running. Jorge Luis Borges, reading the kabbalists in Buenos Aires, called the Torah a cipher of the universe. The universe now replies in the same form.
suggested_refs: The TLS, SSH and IPsec handshakes, the working monument
sources: Absence noted against Wikipedia and award-body records; no contrary source found
